abstract: ABSTRACT Reprimo (encoded by RPRM ) was initially identified as a p53 target gene in 2000 and functions as a tumor suppressor. Promoter hypermethylation of RPRM is frequently observed in various cancers, suggesting that it is transcriptionally silenced during tumorigenesis. Previous studies have reported that overexpression of RPRM induces G2/M cell cycle arrest, inhibits cell proliferation, promotes apoptosis, and increases cellular sensitivity to DNA damage. However, the molecular function of Reprimo is not completely understood. In particular, our recent studies revealed that Reprimo has a novel extracellular function, being secreted outside the cells where it functions to induce apoptosis in its target cells. Furthermore, we found that this apoptosis pathway is novel, mediated by a signaling pathway composed of p53‐Reprimo‐protocadherin family‐Hippo‐YAP/TAZ‐p73. Reprimo is the first example of an extracellular ligand that induces cell death by modulating YAP activity and is a unique upstream regulator of Hippo signaling. This review summarizes current knowledge of the tumor‐suppressive mechanisms of Reprimo, with an emphasis on its unique extracellular function and discusses potential future research directions and clinical applications in cancer therapy.

Introduction
Tumor suppressor genes, such as p53, regulate essential cellular processes that can prevent tumorigenesis, including cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis. Reprimo (
RPRM
) was first identified as a p53‐target gene having cytostatic acitivity [
1
]. Several reports have demonstrated frequent hypermethylation of the
RPRM
promoter across various cancer types, including gastric, breast, pituitary, esophageal, and pancreatic cancers, correlating with reduced gene expression and greater malignancy progression [
2
,
3
,
4
,
5
]. Overexpression of Reprimo leads to tumor‐suppressive responses in several cell types, including G2/M cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, growth defects, and/or migration retardation. However, the molecular mechanisms by which these effects are achieved remain poorly understood. Recently, we have discovered that Reprimo has a novel extracellular function, binding to specific receptors (the protocadherin family members; FAT1, FAT4, CELSR1, CELSR2, and CELSR3) on the surface of cells, inducing dephosphorylation and activation of YAP/TAZ, leading to YAP/TAZ and p73‐dependent apoptosis. These extracellular functions provide new insights into the tumor‐suppressive activities of Reprimo. In this review, we will recapitulate the molecular importance of Reprimo in tumor suppression and propose possible medical applications for the future.
2
Identification of the
RPRM
Gene
Reprimo was first identified as a target of the p53 gene [
1
]. Expression of the
RPRM
gene was initially detected in mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells exposed to X‐ray irradiation, whereas no expression was observed in p53‐deficient (p53−/−) MEF cells, indicating that
RPRM
expression is p53‐dependent. These findings suggested a role for Reprimo downstream of p53. Western blotting analysis showed that the Reprimo protein appears as multiple bands that are sensitive to glycopeptidase F digestion, suggesting extensive post‐translational glycosylation. This modification may regulate the stability, localization, and function of Reprimo.
Functional studies demonstrated that overexpression of N‐terminally HA‐tagged Reprimo induces G2/M cell cycle arrest. This arrest was mediated by inhibition of CDC2 kinase activity and nuclear translocation of the CDC2‐cyclin B1 complex, thereby blocking mitotic entry. Immunofluorescence staining showed that HA‐tagged Reprimo protein predominantly localizes to the cytoplasm in HeLa cells. This initial report on Reprimo thus detailed some molecular functions of Reprimo and indicated its potential role in tumor suppression (Figure
1A
).

3
Expression of
RPRM
mRNA
in Normal and Cancer Tissues
According to data from the Human Protein Atlas (
https://www.proteinatlas.org
),
RPRM
mRNA is highly expressed in the brain, endocrine tissues, gastrointestinal tract, and female reproductive organs, whereas its expression is low in the lung, liver, and pancreas [
6
]. In zebrafish, teleost‐specific genome duplication has given rise to two orthologues of the
RPRM
gene:
RPRM‐a
and
RPRM‐b
. Organ‐specific expression of
RPRM
in humans and zebrafish was examined by in situ hybridization and found in the brain, vasculature, and the digestive tract [
7
]. The close similarity in tissue distribution between humans and zebrafish suggests that
RPRM
function is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrate species.
Promoter hypermethylation is a well‐established mechanism for silencing tumor suppressor genes in various cancers [
8
]. The cytosine residue in CpG dinucleotides is covalently modified by methylation, a modification that is stably maintained through successive rounds of DNA replication by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs). Genomic regions enriched in CpG dinucleotides are called CpG islands. The promoter region of the
RPRM
gene harbors a number of CpG islands. In a clinical study, frequent methylation of the
RPRM
promoter was found in many types of cancers (Table
1
). Although some studies reported increased expression of
RPRM
[

,
17

,

,
15
]. These studies suggest that analysis of promoter methylation in cell‐free serum or plasma samples may be useful for the early detection of cancer, especially gastric cancer [

Taken together, these findings suggest that promoter methylation‐mediated silencing of
RPRM
plays a significant role in cancer development and progression and indicates its role as a tumor suppressor in vivo.
4
Molecular Function of Reprimo Inside of the Cell
Overexpression of
RPRM
leads to G2/M cell cycle arrest in various human cancer cell lines including DLD1, HeLa, Lovo, MCF7, and Saos2, and mouse NIH3T3 cells [
1
]. Other studies report that
RPRM
overexpression induces apoptosis and reduced proliferation in gastric cancer AZ521 and AGS, pituitary tumors LbT2 and GH3 (Figure
1A
) [
3
,
22
,
27
]. On the other hand, overexpression of
RPRM
in breast cancer MDA‐MB‐231 resulted in reduced cell migration and invasion but did not affect the growth rate or lead to cell cycle arrest [
17
].
Overexpression of
RPRM
enhances apoptosis induced by the DNA‐damaging agents 5‐FU and CDDP, which induce DNA double‐strand break (DSB) [
3
]. ATM (ataxia telangiectasia mutated) is one of the most important protein kinases involved in the regulation of the DNA damage response to DSBs [
28
]. Zhang et al. found that Reprimo protein translocates from the cytoplasm to the nucleus shortly after X‐ray irradiation, where it interacts with ATM, followed by nuclear export and proteasomal degradation [
29
]. They found that
RPRM
overexpression results in higher sensitivity to DNA damage due to ATM degradation. Conversely,
RPRM
knockdown increases resistance to X‐ray‐induced DNA damage. From this, the authors concluded that
RPRM
overexpression impairs the DNA repair pathway and renders cells vulnerable to DNA damage, potentially explaining the tumor suppressive role of Reprimo (Figure
1B
).
In gastric cancer,
RPRM
expression correlates with the transcription of S100A2, Survivin, and a long noncoding RNA LINC00467. A positive correlation was found between
RPRM
and S100A2 expression (Figure
1C
) [
30
]. S100A2 is induced by p53 and plays various roles in differentiation, cell growth, and survival [
31
]. A negative correlation was found between
RPRM
vs. Survivin and
RPRM
vs. LINC00467 expression (Figure
1C
) [
30
,
32
,
33
]. Expression levels of Survivin and LINC00467 are increased in several types of cancers. These correlations indicate that expression levels of
RPRM
might be used to predict cancer malignancy.
Overexpression of
RPRM
also leads to Reprimo protein secretion from cells [
34
], and it can be difficult to distinguish the phenotypes caused by cytoplasmic versus extracellular Reprimo activity. We thus examined if extracellular Reprimo plays a role in the reduced cell proliferation or increased apoptosis observed in
RPRM
‐expressing cells.
5
Reprimo Is Secreted by Cells and Induces Apoptosis
Cell death can be classified into several types according to its molecular features [
35
]. The intrinsic apoptosis pathway is evoked in response to severe internal stresses like DNA damage. The extrinsic apoptosis pathway is initiated from protein ligands that interact with receptors on the cell membrane. The tumor necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily is well‐characterized protein ligands that induce extrinsic apoptosis. TNF‐α, TNF‐related apoptosis‐inducing ligand (TRAIL), and FAS/CD95 ligand (FASL/CD95L) bind to multiple receptors, including several death receptors (DRs) that trigger apoptosis in the recipient cells [
36
]. Although there is no obvious sequence similarity between Reprimo and members of the TNF superfamily, we found that Reprimo shares functional similarities with these extrinsic apoptosis inducers [
34
].
As Reprimo protein is highly glycosylated, we suspected that it may be secreted from cells. When we transfected HEK293T cells with a C‐terminally FLAG‐tagged Reprimo‐expressing vector, we found that Reprimo protein was detected in both whole cell extracts and the extracellular culture media, confirming the secretion of Reprimo. We next investigated if this secreted Reprimo protein contributed to its tumor suppressing function. We found that viability was strongly reduced in four cell lines (HeLa, ACHN, H1299, and HEK293) when incubated in the presence of soluble Reprimo protein. HeLa cells incubated in the presence of recombinant Reprimo protein showed features typical of apoptosis such as genomic DNA fragmentation and caspase 3 activation. We found that fibroblast cells derived from human (IMR‐90) were tolerant to cell death caused by Reprimo protein. Thus, the ability of Reprimo to induce cell death appears to depend on cell type, and the mechanism underlying the resistance of IMR‐90 cells to Reprimo remains to be elucidated (Figure
2A
).

(C) HeLa cells were mixed with human normal fibroblasts expressing
RPRM
. The mixed cells were injected subcutaneously into both ventral sides of nude mice. HeLa cells mixed with

overexpressing fibroblast suppresses tumor formation.
6
Identification of Reprimo Receptors;
FAT1
,
FAT4
,
CELSR1
,
CELSR2
, and
CELSR3
To investigate which receptor(s) mediate the extracellular function of Reprimo, we used immunoprecipitation and mass‐spectrometry (IP‐MS). We found that Reprimo protein was not tightly attached to the cell surface, indicating a transient interaction. We next used the bifunctional crosslinker Sulfo‐LC‐SDA to probe this possible interaction. Sulfo‐LC‐SDA has two arms: one which contains an NHS ester and the other a diazirine. NHS esters are reactive groups that form stable conjugates with primary amines. Diazirines are photo‐activatable chemical groups that form stable conjugates with any amino acid side chain or peptide backbone after UV irradiation. We reacted soluble Reprimo protein with the NHS ester arm of Sulfo‐LC‐SDA, then incubated these pre‐formed conjugates with live cells, followed by UV irradiation. Finally, we used IP‐MS to analyze the complexes between Reprimo and the putative cross‐linked surface receptors. Among the proteins identified were members of the protocadherin family: FAT1, FAT4, CELSR1, CELSR2, and CELSR3 (Figure
2B
). This would represent the first identified extracellular ligand for the protocadherin family, which has been classically recognized for its roles in cell–cell adhesion and planar cell polarity but has not been reported to have extracellular ligands. This novel interaction suggests that protocadherins not only function in cell structure but also participate in ligand‐mediated signaling cascades that influence tumor cell behavior.
7
An Extrinsic Cell‐Death‐Inducing Signaling Pathway Comprised of p53, Reprimo,
FAT1
/
FAT4
/
CELSR1
/
CELSR2
/
CELSR3
,
YAP
/
TAZ
, and p73
FAT1 and FAT4 function upstream in the Hippo signaling pathway, and CELSR2 enhances YAP/TAZ activation [
37
,
38
,
39
]. When HEK293 cells were incubated with Reprimo protein, phosphorylation levels of YAP were dramatically reduced. We observed YAP accumulation in the nucleus and activation of YAP‐TEAD target genes in these cells. Although further study is required to elucidate the precise relationship between Reprimo and YAP, it is clear that extrinsic Reprimo protein induces Hippo‐YAP signaling. YAP has been shown to associate with p73 to induce apoptosis [
40
,
41
], and we detected upregulation of p73‐ and p53‐target genes following incubation with Reprimo protein. From these results, we hypothesized the existence of a signaling axis consisting of p53‐Reprimo‐Hippo‐YAP/TAZ‐p73. In this cascade, p53 first activates
RPRM
expression, and Reprimo protein is secreted from cells. Next, Reprimo protein interacts with protocadherin family members on the surface of both the secreting and nearby cells. This causes YAP to translocate and accumulate in the nucleus of the stimulated cells, where it interacts with p73, which then activates apoptotic genes. Finally, this induces apoptosis in the Reprimo‐stimulated cells. Consistent with this hypothesis, knockdown of YAP, TAZ, CELSR2, or p73 was found to attenuate cell death induced by Reprimo protein.
8
In Vivo Tumor Suppressive Function of Reprimo
Ooki et al. investigated whether
RPRM
overexpression suppresses tumor growth in mouse xenograft models. They found that gastric cancer AZ521 cells transfected with a
RPRM
‐expressing vector formed significantly smaller tumors compared to mock‐transfected controls [
3
]. These results can be interpreted as the consequence of the combined effects of both internal and external Reprimo. Reprimo may act via an autocrine mechanism, whereby secreted Reprimo protein binds to surface receptors on the same cells that produce it, or via a paracrine mechanism, affecting neighboring cells. To evaluate its paracrine activity, we performed xenograft experiments in which HeLa cells were co‐injected with fibroblasts expressing Reprimo. Tumor growth was significantly suppressed when HeLa cells were mixed with fibroblasts exogenously expressing
RPRM
, indicating that secreted Reprimo from neighboring fibroblasts inhibits cancer cell proliferation via a paracrine mechanism (Figure
2C
). Consistently, co‐injection with
RPRM
‐knockout fibroblasts resulted in larger tumors compared to those mixed with wild‐type fibroblasts that endogenously express
RPRM
. These findings collectively demonstrate that loss of
RPRM
promotes tumor formation in vivo.
In line with these functional observations, promoter methylation and loss of
RPRM
expression are frequently found in several types of cancer. A query of the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) Pan‐Cancer database revealed that
RPRM
expression levels are reduced in various cancer types (12 out of 16 cancer types) [
34
]. Taken together, we concluded that secreted Reprimo suppresses tumorigenesis via autocrine and/or paracrine stimulation in vivo (Figure
3
).
FIGURE 3
An extrinsic cell‐death‐inducing signaling pathway comprised of p53, Reprimo, FAT1/FAT4/CELSR1/CELSR2/CELSR3, YAP/TAZ, and p73. RPRM expression is activated by p53. Reprimo protein is secreted from cells, where it specifically interacts with the protocadherin family members FAT1, FAT4, CELSR1, CELSR2, and/or CELSR3. This causes a decrease in the phosphorylation of YAP, which translocates to nucleus. YAP‐p73 then modulates the expression of apoptosis‐related genes leading to cell apoptosis.
9
Clinical Implications and Future Applications
The promoter region of
RPRM
is methylated in gastric cancer and could be a useful marker for predicting cancer malignancy [
10
]. Indeed, some reports have shown that the methylation state of
RPRM
DNA can be utilized as a biomarker for detecting gastric cancer [
42
]. In addition to gastric cancer, patients with pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, or AML show a correlation between
RPRM
methylation and worse prognosis (Table
1
). The methylation state of
RPRM
might further be useful for cancer grading and prognosis assessment.
As p53 promotes DNA repair, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis, it plays a key role in suppressing tumorigenesis. Reprimo, acting downstream of p53, also contributes to tumor suppression through both its cytoplasmic and extracellular functions. We observed that extracellular Reprimo protein strongly induces apoptosis in cancer cell lines, whereas fibroblasts remain resistant to Reprimo‐induced apoptosis (Figure
2A
). Thus, secreted Reprimo may selectively induce apoptosis in tumor cells, contributing to tumor suppression (Figure
4A
).
FIGURE 4
Proposed functions of reprimo in clinical contexts. (A) In the precancerous state, cells expressing Reprimo resist aberrant cell proliferation. Cytoplasmic Reprimo promotes cell cycle arrest and suppresses growth. Extracellular Reprimo promotes apoptosis in nearby cells. Loss of TP53 or promoter hypermethylation on
RPRM
leads to loss of Reprimo function. (B) Treatment of tumor cells with ionizing radiation results in the accumulation of DNA damage and activation of p53 and
RPRM
. Reprimo expression suppresses cell growth and promotes apoptosis. Secreted Reprimo protein also induces cell death in a paracrine manner as a bystander effect.
Patients receiving cranial radiotherapy (CRT) for brain tumors often suffer from radiation‐induced brain injury (RIBI) in adjacent normal tissues. Ye et al. reported that knockout of
RPRM
mitigates RIBI [
43
]. Given the extracellular apoptosis‐inducing function of Reprimo, we hypothesize that RIBI may be induced, at least in part, by secreted Reprimo protein (Figure
4B
). When tumor cells are exposed to ionizing radiation (IR), DNA damage accumulates, leading to activation of the p53 pathway and subsequent overexpression of
RPRM
. The secreted Reprimo protein can induce apoptosis not only in irradiated tumor cells but also in neighboring non‐targeted cells—a phenomenon known as the bystander effect [
44
,
45
]. This secondary apoptosis may contribute to RIBI. Based on this hypothesis, removing extracellular Reprimo using specific antibodies or suppressing its secretion after CRT may help prevent RIBI.
Conversely, introducing recombinant Reprimo protein into solid tumors could selectively induce apoptosis in cancer cells while sparing normal fibroblasts. Therefore, modulation of extracellular Reprimo—either enhancing its pro‐apoptotic activity for tumor therapy or inhibiting it to protect surrounding normal tissues—may offer promise as a therapeutic treatment.
10
Conclusion and Discussion
Our recent findings, along with previous studies, have elucidated the tumor‐suppressive functions of Reprimo. Remarkably, Reprimo is the first extracellular protein demonstrated to modulate YAP activity via receptor‐mediated mechanisms. This finding establishes Reprimo as a novel upstream extracellular regulator that directly influences Hippo–YAP signaling output. Through this unique mechanism, Reprimo might convert YAP‐driven proliferative signaling into pro‐apoptotic output, representing a previously unrecognized form of YAP‐dependent tumor suppression. Modulating the expression and secretion of Reprimo could offer promising avenues for novel cancer therapies, including potential applications in radiotherapy modulation and targeted apoptosis induction.
The subcellular localization of Reprimo was initially reported to be cytoplasmic in HeLa cells [
1
]. A recent study demonstrated that N‐terminally HA‐tagged Reprimo accumulates in the nucleus of MEFs in response to X‐ray irradiation [
29
]. In clinical samples, Reprimo has been detected in the cytoplasm of gastric tissues and in the axons of neurons. However, nuclear localization has also been observed in astrocytes, endothelial cells, and other tissue types [
7
,
11
,
30
]. These findings suggest that Reprimo may have context‐dependent localization, and further functional analyses are needed to clarify its roles in both the cytoplasm and the nucleus. Although the latest version of SignalP (
https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/SignalP‐6.0/
) did not predict a signal peptide at the N‐terminus of Reprimo, N‐linked glycosylation has been experimentally confirmed [
1
,
34
]. Computational analysis using NetNGlyc (
https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/NetNGlyc‐1.0/
) predicts glycosylation sites at asparagine residues 7 and 18. Additional studies are warranted to determine whether Reprimo is glycosylated and secreted via the conventional ER‐Golgi pathway or through an unconventional protein secretion mechanism [
46
].
The predominant expression of
RPRM
in tissues such as the brain, endocrine organs, and gastrointestinal tract suggests that Reprimo may play important roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, or tissue homeostasis in these organs under physiological conditions. It is well known that apoptosis is indispensable for brain development [
47
].
RPRM‐a
and
RPRM‐b
expression detected in the zebrafish nervous system during early embryogenesis might induce apoptosis for proper development. Nevertheless, the physiological roles of Reprimo in normal tissues remain largely unexplored. Further investigations, such as examining its apoptotic role during organ development, may uncover additional functions beyond tumor suppression.
